grammar.title: A is B
grammar.explain: The most basic sentence in Japanese. は (pronounced "wa" here) marks the topic, and です politely ends the sentence, like "is."

quiz.en: Mr. Tanaka is a teacher.

grammar.title: is not
grammar.explain: The negative of です. じゃありません is the spoken form; ではありません is a bit more formal. Casual: じゃない.

quiz.en: That person isn't Japanese.

grammar.title: Question marker
grammar.explain: Add か to the end of a polite sentence to turn it into a question. No word order change needed, and Japanese often uses 。 instead of ?.

quiz.en: What is this?

grammar.title: A's B
grammar.explain: の links two nouns — usually possession ("my book"), but also origin or category ("a Japanese car").

quiz.en: That is my mother's bag.

grammar.title: Object marker
grammar.explain: を (pronounced "o") marks what the action is done to — the thing eaten, read, bought. The verb always comes at the end.

quiz.en: I drink coffee every morning.

grammar.title: to (a destination)
grammar.explain: With movement verbs like 行く and 来る, に or へ marks where you're going. へ (said "e") stresses direction; に stresses arrival. Both are fine.
grammar.form: Place に/へ 行く・来る・帰る

quiz.en: Tomorrow I'll go to school.

grammar.title: at (a specific time)
grammar.explain: に marks a specific point in time: clock times, days, dates. Relative words like 今日, 明日, 毎日 don't take に.

examples.en: I'll watch a movie on Sunday.

quiz.en: I go to bed at nine.

grammar.title: at / in (where an action happens)
grammar.explain: で marks where an action takes place. Compare: に is where something exists or goes; で is where something is done.

quiz.en: I ate lunch at a restaurant.

grammar.title: by / with / in (a tool or method)
grammar.explain: で also marks the means of doing something: transport, tools, languages.

examples.en: I go to work by bus.

quiz.en: I eat with chopsticks.

grammar.title: A and B / with
grammar.explain: と joins nouns into a complete list ("A and B"). After a person, it means "with." It can't join verbs or sentences.

examples.en: I saw a movie with a friend.

quiz.en: I went shopping with my older sister.

grammar.title: also / too
grammar.explain: も replaces は, が, or を to mean "also." With a negative, it means "(not) either."

examples.en: I eat neither meat nor fish.

quiz.en: My younger sister likes cats too.

grammar.pattern: 〜が あります / います
grammar.title: there is / I have
grammar.explain: Both mean "there is." Use あります for things and plants, います for people and animals. が marks what exists.
grammar.form: Place に Noun が あります/います

examples.en: There's a book on the desk.
There's a dog in the park.

quiz.en: There are students in the classroom.

grammar.title: polite verb form
grammar.explain: ます makes a verb polite and non-past (present or future). Negative: ません. Past: ました. Past negative: ませんでした.
grammar.form: Verb stem + ます / ません / ました

quiz.en: I met a friend yesterday.

grammar.title: let's ~
grammar.explain: Swap ます for ましょう to suggest doing something together. As a question (ましょうか) it offers help: "Shall I ~?"

quiz.en: Let's take a short break.

grammar.title: won't you ~? (invitation)
grammar.explain: A soft, polite invitation — literally "won't you ~?" It sounds gentler than ましょう because it leaves room to say no.

examples.en: Would you like to go see a movie?

quiz.en: Want to go out together this weekend?

grammar.title: want to ~
grammar.explain: Attach たい to a verb stem to say you want to do it. It conjugates like an い-adjective: たくない (don't want to), たかった (wanted to).

examples.en: I want to go to Japan.
I don't want to eat anything today.

quiz.en: I want to buy new shoes.

grammar.title: please do ~
grammar.explain: The て-form of a verb + ください is a polite request. For "please don't," use ないでください.

quiz.en: Please say it one more time.

grammar.title: is ~ing / ongoing state
grammar.explain: て-form + いる describes an action in progress ("is eating") or a resulting state ("is married," "lives in").
grammar.form: Verb て-form + いる/います

examples.en: My older sister lives in Osaka.

quiz.en: My little brother is sleeping in his room.

grammar.title: it's okay to ~ / may I ~?
grammar.explain: て-form + もいい gives permission. Add ですか to ask for it.
grammar.form: Verb て-form + もいいです(か)

quiz.en: May I enter this room?

grammar.title: must not ~
grammar.explain: て-form + はいけません forbids something. You'll see it on signs and hear it from teachers and parents.
grammar.form: Verb て-form + はいけません

examples.en: You mustn't talk in the library.

quiz.en: You must not run at the pool.

grammar.title: adjective past tense
grammar.explain: い-adjectives swap い for かった (楽しい → 楽しかった). な-adjectives and nouns use でした (静か → 静かでした). Exception: いい → よかった.
grammar.form: い-adj: 〜かった / な-adj: 〜でした

quiz.en: It was cold yesterday.

grammar.title: adjective negative
grammar.explain: い-adjectives swap い for くない (高い → 高くない). な-adjectives use じゃない (好き → 好きじゃない). Exception: いい → よくない.
grammar.form: い-adj: 〜くない / な-adj: 〜じゃない

quiz.en: It isn't very hot today.

grammar.title: to like ~
grammar.explain: 好き is an adjective, not a verb — so the thing you like takes が, not を. Same for 嫌い, 上手, 下手, and 分かる.

examples.en: My older brother is good at cooking.

quiz.en: I like dogs.

grammar.title: because ~
grammar.explain: から after a clause gives the reason. The reason comes first, the result second — the opposite of English "because."

examples.en: It's cold, so I'll close the window.
We don't have time, so let's take a taxi.

quiz.en: It's raining, so I'm staying home.

grammar.title: from ~ until/to ~
grammar.explain: から marks a starting point and まで an end point, for both time and place.
grammar.form: A から B まで

examples.en: I work from nine to five.
I walk from home to the station.

quiz.en: I have school from Monday to Friday.

grammar.title: right? / you know!
grammar.explain: ね seeks agreement about something you both know ("isn't it?"). よ tells the listener something new ("I'm telling you").

examples.en: This place is good, you know!

quiz.en: (Looking together, seeking agreement) Pretty flowers, aren't they?

grammar.title: topic vs subject
grammar.explain: は sets the topic ("as for X…") and puts the focus on what comes after. が puts the focus on the subject itself — used for new info and in question-word answers: 誰が来ましたか → 田中さんが来ました.
grammar.form: Known topic は… / New info が…

quiz.en: Who came?

grammar.title: ~ and then ~
grammar.explain: The て-form links actions in order: "do A, and then B." Only the last verb shows the tense.

examples.en: I get up in the morning and take a shower.
I went home and ate dinner.

quiz.en: I wash my hands and then eat.

grammar.title: before ~ing
grammar.explain: Dictionary-form verb + 前に means "before doing." With a noun, use の前に (食事の前に).

examples.en: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Let's wash our hands before the meal.

quiz.en: Please close the windows before you go out.

grammar.title: after ~ing
grammar.explain: Past-form (た) verb + 後で means "after doing." With a noun, use の後で (授業の後で).

examples.en: I'll play games after doing my homework.
After class, I'm going to the library.

quiz.en: After eating, I went for a walk.

grammar.title: have (ever) done ~
grammar.explain: た-form + ことがある talks about past experience: things you've done at least once.
grammar.form: Verb (た-form) + ことがあります

quiz.en: I've been to Japan.

grammar.title: do things like ~ and ~
grammar.explain: Lists a few example activities out of many, unlike て which lists them in order. End with する.
grammar.form: Verb たり、Verb たり する

examples.en: On weekends I do things like read and watch movies.
Yesterday I cleaned, did laundry, and so on.

quiz.en: On days off I go shopping, cook, and so on.

grammar.title: while ~ing
grammar.explain: Verb stem + ながら means doing two things at once. The main action goes last.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
Please don't talk on the phone while walking.

quiz.en: I eat while watching TV.

grammar.title: can ~ (potential form)
grammar.explain: Ichidan verbs: る → られる (食べられる). Godan verbs: final u-sound → e-sound + る (話す → 話せる). Irregular: する → できる, 来る → 来られる.
grammar.form: 食べる → 食べられる / 書く → 書ける

examples.en: I can read a little kanji.

quiz.en: I can't swim.

grammar.title: if / when ~
grammar.explain: た-form + ら means "if" or "once ~ happens." It's the most flexible conditional and very common in speech.

examples.en: Call me when you get to the station.
If it rains, I won't go.

quiz.en: If you have time, come visit.

grammar.title: even if ~
grammar.explain: て-form + も means "even if" or "even though" — the result happens regardless.

examples.en: I'll go even if it rains.
No matter how many times I hear it, I don't get it.

quiz.en: Even if it's expensive, I'll buy it.

grammar.title: because ~ (softer)
grammar.explain: Like から but softer and more objective, so it's preferred for polite excuses and explanations. After a noun or な-adjective, use なので.
grammar.form: Clause + ので / Noun + なので

examples.en: I have a fever, so I'll take today off.
Tomorrow is Sunday, so there's no school.

quiz.en: I have a headache, so I'll head home first.

grammar.title: you'd better ~ / should ~
grammar.explain: た-form + ほうがいい gives advice. For "better not," use ないほうがいい.

examples.en: You should go to bed early.

quiz.en: You should go to the hospital.

grammar.title: must / have to ~
grammar.explain: Literally "if I don't do it, it won't do." In speech it often shrinks to なきゃ or なくちゃ.
grammar.form: Verb ない-stem + なければなりません

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

quiz.en: I have to do my homework.

grammar.title: I heard that ~
grammar.explain: Plain form + そうです reports what you heard or read. Don't mix it up with stem + そう ("looks like").

examples.en: I hear it's going to snow tomorrow.

quiz.en: I heard Tanaka is getting married next month.

grammar.title: looks ~
grammar.explain: Adjective stem + そう means "looks ~" based on what you see: おいしい → おいしそう. Exception: いい → よさそう.
grammar.form: い-adj (drop い) / な-adj + そう

examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain.

quiz.en: That luggage looks heavy.

grammar.title: end up ~ / (oops) did ~
grammar.explain: て-form + しまう shows something is completely done, often with regret. Casual: 〜ちゃう.

examples.en: I ate the whole cake. Oops.

quiz.en: I left my umbrella on the train (ugh).

grammar.title: try ~ing
grammar.explain: て-form + みる means "try doing it and see." It comes from 見る (to see).

examples.en: I'd like to try going to Japan once.

quiz.en: Try eating this ramen.

grammar.pattern: あげる / くれる / もらう
grammar.title: giving and receiving
grammar.explain: あげる: I (or my side) give outward. くれる: someone gives to me. もらう: I receive. The direction matters more than who holds the item.
grammar.form: A は B に X を あげる / くれる / もらう

examples.en: My friend gave me a book.

quiz.en: The teacher gave me a dictionary.

grammar.title: I'm thinking of ~ing
grammar.explain: Volitional form (行こう, 食べよう) + と思う shares an intention or plan you've been considering.

examples.en: I'm thinking of studying abroad in Japan next year.
I'm planning to go to bed early tonight.

quiz.en: I'm thinking of going to the beach this weekend.

facts.title: Three scripts, one sentence
facts.body: Japanese mixes hiragana (grammar and native words), katakana (loanwords and emphasis), and kanji (meaning-carrying characters) — often all in one line.

example.en: I like coffee. — 私 and 好 are kanji, コーヒー is katakana, the rest is hiragana.

facts.title: Why は is read "wa"
facts.body: As a particle, は is pronounced "wa" and へ is pronounced "e" — leftovers from older spelling. Everywhere else they're "ha" and "he" as usual.

example.en: Today is sunny. — 今日は = "kyou wa".

facts.title: The verb comes last
facts.body: Japanese is subject–object–verb. You often don't know what's happening until the very end of the sentence — which is why listening to the end matters.

example.en: I eat bread every morning. (lit. I every-morning bread eat.)

facts.title: Subjects are optional
facts.body: If it's clear from context who's doing something, Japanese just leaves it out. Saying 私は over and over sounds unnatural.

example.en: (I) watched a movie yesterday.

facts.title: No plurals (mostly)
facts.body: Nouns don't change for number: 本 is "book" or "books." Context, numbers, or 〜たち (for people) fill the gap.

example.en: I bought three books.

facts.title: Counting depends on shape
facts.body: Japanese counts things with counters: 本 for long thin things (pens, bottles), 枚 for flat things (paper, shirts), 匹 for small animals, 冊 for books.

example.en: There are two pens.

facts.title: いただきます
facts.body: Said before eating — a humble "I receive this." After the meal, say ごちそうさまでした to thank whoever made or paid for it.

example.en: (Before eating) Thank you for this food!

facts.title: Three levels of politeness
facts.body: Casual (食べる), polite (食べます), and honorific/humble (召し上がる／いただく). Learners start with ます-form: it's safe with almost anyone.

example.en: What will you eat? (polite, safe default)

facts.title: 〜さん isn't for yourself
facts.body: さん is a polite suffix for other people's names — never your own. Kids get 〜ちゃん or 〜くん; teachers and doctors get 〜先生.

example.en: Good morning, Mr./Ms. Tanaka.

facts.title: A language full of sound effects
facts.body: Japanese has thousands of mimetic words — not just sounds but feelings and textures. ドキドキ (heart pounding), キラキラ (sparkling), ペコペコ (starving).

example.en: I'm starving.

facts.title: Pitch changes meaning
facts.body: Japanese uses pitch, not stress. はし with high-low pitch is 箸 (chopsticks); low-high is 橋 (bridge). Context usually saves you.

example.en: I eat with chopsticks.

facts.title: Katakana English
facts.body: Loanwords get Japanese sounds: コンビニ (convenience store), パソコン (personal computer), スマホ (smartphone). Many are clipped to 4 syllables.

example.en: I charged my phone at the convenience store.

facts.title: English that isn't English
facts.body: Some katakana words were made up in Japan: サラリーマン (office worker), マイペース (doing things at your own pace), ペーパードライバー (licensed but never drives).

example.en: He does things at his own pace.

facts.title: Kanji have several readings
facts.body: Most kanji have a Chinese-derived on'yomi and a native kun'yomi. 山 alone is やま (mountain), but in 富士山 it's さん.

example.en: Mt. Fuji is a tall mountain.

facts.title: Kanji + hiragana tails
facts.body: Verbs and adjectives write their core in kanji and the changing part in hiragana (okurigana), so conjugation is easy to see: 食べる → 食べた → 食べない.

example.en: I already ate.

facts.title: すみません does triple duty
facts.body: It means "excuse me" (to get attention), "sorry" (small apology), and even "thank you" when someone went out of their way for you.

example.en: Sorry for the trouble — thank you so much.

facts.title: よろしくお願いします
facts.body: No neat English equivalent: "please treat me well / I'm counting on you." Said when meeting people, starting work together, or asking favors.

example.en: Nice to meet you. (I look forward to getting along.)

facts.title: Listening out loud
facts.body: Japanese listeners give constant feedback called aizuchi — はい, ええ, そうですね, なるほど — to show they're following. Silence can seem like you aren't.

example.en: I see, is that so.

facts.title: Dates have special readings
facts.body: The first ten days of the month use native readings: 一日 is ついたち, 二日 ふつか, 三日 みっか… 十日 とおか. Also 二十日 はつか.

example.en: April 1st is a Sunday.

facts.title: Days of the week are the planets
facts.body: 月 moon, 火 fire (Mars), 水 water (Mercury), 木 wood (Jupiter), 金 gold (Venus), 土 earth (Saturn), 日 sun — just like the old Latin names.

example.en: Let's meet on Friday.

facts.title: The こそあど system
facts.body: こ = near me, そ = near you, あ = over there, ど = which/question. It works across words: これ／それ／あれ／どれ, ここ／そこ／あそこ／どこ.

example.en: The restroom is over there.

facts.title: No future tense
facts.body: Japanese only marks past vs. non-past. 行きます covers both "I go" and "I will go" — time words make it clear.

example.en: I'll go to Kyoto next week.

facts.title: Feelings as weather
facts.body: Japanese often describes feelings as states rather than actions: 寂しい (lonely), 懐かしい (nostalgic), もったいない (what a waste!). Some don't translate cleanly.

example.en: It still works — what a waste to throw it out!

facts.title: ただいま／おかえり
facts.body: Coming home, you say ただいま ("I'm back"). Whoever's home answers おかえり ("welcome back"). It's a small daily ritual.

example.en: I'm home! — Welcome back.

facts.title: The genkan
facts.body: Homes have a genkan, a lowered entry area where you take off your shoes. Stepping up onto the floor means you've really come inside.

example.en: Please take your shoes off here.

facts.title: Kanji are built from parts
facts.body: Many kanji combine a meaning part (radical) with a sound part. 氵 relates to water: 海 sea, 池 pond, 泳 swim, 洗 wash.

example.en: I swam in the sea.

facts.title: Casual speech drops a lot
facts.body: Among friends, です and ます disappear, particles get dropped, and questions end in a rising tone instead of か.

example.en: Want to eat this?

facts.title: What N5 → N1 means
facts.body: The JLPT is Japan's standard proficiency test. N5 is the basics (~800 words, ~100 kanji); N1 is near-native (~10,000 words, ~2,000 kanji).

example.en: I'm taking the N4 next year.

facts.title: Why words come back
facts.body: Nagare quizzes you right before you'd forget, then waits longer each time you get it right. That spacing is what moves words into long-term memory.

sentences.en: I like Sundays.
In the morning, I get up at nine.
Then I eat breakfast.
In the afternoon, I go to the park.
I take a walk with my dog.
It's really fun.
In the evening, I eat dinner with my family.
After that, I watch TV.
I go to bed early.
I have a father, a mother, and an older brother.
My father is an office worker.
Every morning, he goes to the office early.
My mother is good at cooking.
Dinner is always delicious.
My older brother is a student.
He's studying English now.
Everyone is doing well.
Today I went shopping at the supermarket with my mother.
We bought apples, fish, and eggs.
It wasn't very expensive.
Then we bought new shoes, too.
It was a lot of fun.
We went home and everyone made dinner together.
There's a white cat at the house next door.
Her name is Yuki.
Every morning, Yuki comes into my garden.
She sleeps lazily under the flowers.
I give Yuki some water.
Yuki doesn't say anything, but she's very cute.
In the evening, Yuki goes back to her own home.
She'll probably come again tomorrow.
There's a small café in front of the station.
It's an old place, but very quiet.
I come here every Saturday.
I always order coffee and cake.
The old man who runs the shop is very kind.
Today the old man said, "Thanks for always coming."
I was happy and smiled a little.
Last year, I went to Japan for the first time.
In Tokyo, I went into a sushi restaurant with a friend.
The sushi was going around on little plates.
I didn't know which one to take.
My friend said, "Try this one."
It was salmon.
It was really delicious.
That day, I ate a whole ten plates.
Last week, I made plans with a friend to travel to Kyoto.
We set off from the station early in the morning.
Kyoto is very peaceful, and has lots of famous temples.
We looked at old temples and took lots of photos.
The view from the windows was unusual and beautiful too.
After that, we learned a little about Kyoto's culture.
We ate delicious food, too.
At night, my friend and I talked about all sorts of things at the hotel.
It was a fun trip.
There have been a lot of rainy days lately.
This morning, too, it was raining when I got up.
I took an umbrella and walked to the station.
It was a bit of a hassle, but I pushed through.
The train was more crowded than usual, and I got a little tired.
When I got to the office, a friend gave me some tea.
That made me happy.
In the afternoon, the rain stopped and the sky got brighter.
After work, I met a friend I hadn't seen in a while, and we ate together.
Yesterday, I left my wallet on the train.
I only noticed after I got home.
I got really worried and called the station right away.
The station staff listened carefully to me.
The next day, I got a call saying, "Your wallet has been turned in."
The money and cards were all still inside.
They say lost things often come back in Japan.
I felt truly grateful.
I've been studying Japanese since last year.
At first, even memorizing hiragana was hard.
But I kept at it a little every day.
Recently, I've become able to read simple books.
I look up words I don't know in the dictionary right away.
Kanji is still hard, but it's interesting.
Someday, I'd like to try working in Japan.
It's been decided that I'm moving to a new apartment next month.
That's because my current room is far from the station, which was inconvenient.
The new apartment is a five-minute walk from the station.
The room is a little small, but you can see a park from the window.
On the weekend, a friend helped me get ready.
It took a whole day to pack my books and clothes into boxes.
To thank my friend, I treated them to dinner.
I'm looking forward to my new life.
